You use the conditional: I would like, could you, I would do… for wishes, politeness, advice and imaginary situations.
I would like to travel all over the world.
If I were you, I wouldn’t buy it.
To form the conditional: hablaría, comería, viviría.
To use the irregular forms (the same as in the future): tendría, haría, podría, diría…
To ask for things very politely: ¿Podría…? ¿Le importaría…?
To give advice: deberías, yo que tú, en tu lugar.
To talk about wishes and imaginary situations: me gustaría, ¿qué harías?
In Spain, on 22 December, everyone follows the Christmas lottery, “El Gordo”. The friends have bought a ticket together.
We’ve got our Christmas ticket! If we win the big prize, what would you do?
I’d quit my job and travel around the world. I’d start with Japan, of course.
I wouldn’t quit my job; I love being a doctor. But I’d buy a house in the mountains in Romania.
And you wouldn’t do anything crazy? A sports car? A yacht?
Well… maybe a new car. Mine is fifteen years old.
I’d open a second restaurant, in Barcelona. And I’d give part of it to an NGO.
How generous! I’d love to study music in Vienna. It’s always been my dream.
But guys, the prize isn’t that big: the ticket costs twenty euros and split four ways… we’d get a hundred thousand euros each.
A hundred thousand? Well… if I were you, I wouldn’t quit your job, Ana.
Ha, ha. You’re right. Then I’d take a short trip… to Japan.
And I’d take you to my city, Osaka. We could stay with my parents.
I’d love that! Could you teach us to make real sushi?
Of course. But first… we have to win the lottery!

The conditional is stressed on “RÍ”: a-bla-RÍ-a, ten-DRÍ-a, goos-ta-RÍ-a.
Watch the difference: hablaré (I will speak) / hablaría (I would speak). Only the ending changes: -é / -ía.
Stress on the first syllable: DÉ-ci-mo. And “Gordo” with a single tapped r.
1. The conditional: “I would speak, I would eat”
It’s formed exactly like the future: the whole infinitive + endings. The only difference is that the endings are -ía (like the imperfect of -er verbs).
English forms the conditional with “would”: I would speak. Spanish attaches it to the end: hablar-ía. Same meaning!
2. The irregulars: the same as in the future!
The good news: if you know the irregular future (chapter 21), you know the conditional too. Same stem, different endings:
The conditional makes any request more polite. It’s the perfect form for shops, offices and strangers:
Would you mind letting me through?
Remember “quería” (imperfect) from chapter 24? It’s polite too. The order of politeness: quiero < quería < querría / me gustaría.
If I were you, I wouldn’t go.
In your place, I would accept.
“Deberías” is gentler than “tienes que” (chapter 23). It’s a friend’s advice, not an order.
The conditional describes what would happen in an imaginary world:
What would you do with a million euros?
I would travel all over the world.
With more time, I would learn Japanese.
The full sentence “If I had…, I would…” needs a new tense in Spanish (si TUVIERA…, haría), which you learn at B1. For now use “con…”, “en tu lugar”, “yo que tú” or just the conditional.
In the dialogue you saw “Si nos toca, ¿qué haríais?”: native speakers sometimes say it like that in relaxed conversation, but the correct form is “Si nos tocara”.
“I will speak” or “I would speak”? → “I would speak.”
Me gustaría un té, por favor.
I would love to study music in Vienna.
El Gordo: la lotería más famosa
Why all of Spain stops on the morning of 22 December.
Every 22 December, millions of Spaniards turn on the TV in the morning.
They’re not watching the news: they’re listening to children singing numbers for hours.
It’s the Christmas Lottery draw, which has existed since 1812.
The biggest prize is called “el Gordo” (the Fat One). For a twenty-euro ticket, you win four hundred thousand.
The interesting thing is that almost nobody plays alone: tickets are shared with family, workmates or friends from the bar.
That’s why, when it’s won, a whole village or a whole office wins.
Many winners say the same thing: “I’d pay off the mortgage and help my children.”
Few say they would quit their job.
Those who don’t win have their own phrase too: “The important thing is that we’re healthy.”
And you? Would you buy a ticket? Who would you share it with?
And most importantly: if you won, what would you do?
“el Gordo” = the fat one (the big prize)
On 22 December, at eleven in the morning, Kenji’s phone wouldn’t stop ringing. It was his group of friends.
“We’ve won! We’ve won!”, Lena was shouting. The ticket they had bought together had won ten thousand euros.
It wasn’t the big prize, but it was a lot of money: two thousand five hundred euros each.
Kenji smiled. He had the ticket. He had put it somewhere safe… but where?
He looked in his wallet. It wasn’t there. He looked in the kitchen drawers, under the bed, in the pockets of all his jackets. Nothing.
An hour later his friends came round to celebrate. Kenji was pale.
“Guys, I have a problem,” he said. “I can’t find the ticket.”
There was a terrible silence. Then everyone started giving advice at the same time.
“If I were you, I’d look at the restaurant,” said Ana. “You should think about what you did on the day you bought it,” said Mihai.
Tom said nothing. He just looked out of the window, very seriously.
Kenji closed his eyes. That day he had bought the ticket in the morning. Then he had been to the market. Then he had cooked…
Suddenly he opened his eyes. “The recipe book!”, he shouted. He ran to the shelf and took down a big Japanese cookbook.
He opened it at the ramen page and there was the ticket, slightly stained with soy sauce.
Everyone cheered. Lena hugged Kenji. Mihai opened a bottle of cava.
“So what would you do with the money?”, asked Ana. “I’d buy a new bike,” said Tom. “I’d pay for the music course in Vienna,” said Lena.
Mihai looked at Ana and said: “I’d save it for a very special trip.”
Kenji put the ticket in a safe. “This time,” he said, “I wouldn’t put it in a recipe book for anything.”
The next day they all went together to collect the prize. At the counter, the clerk looked at the stained ticket and asked: “Is that soy sauce?”.
“It’s a very long story,” Kenji answered. And they all started laughing again.
That evening, each of them went home with their share of the prize and a story to tell for years.
“no paraba de sonar” = wouldn’t stop ringing

Text to read: The advice column
A reader asks a magazine for advice.
Dear Clara, I’m thirty and I work at a bank, but I’m terribly bored.
I would love to be a photographer. Should I quit my job? Marta.
Dear Marta, if I were you, I wouldn’t quit just yet.
You could do a photography course at weekends and start working at weddings.
When you have enough clients, it would be the time to change. Good luck! Clara.
